content: The Pit of Despair, also known as the vertical chamber, was a device used in experiments conducted on rhesus macaque monkeys during the 1970s by American comparative psychologist Harry Harlow and his students at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The purpose of these experiments was to create an animal model of human clinical depression. The vertical chamber was essentially a stainless-steel trough with sloping sides that led to a rounded bottom. A wire mesh floor, positioned about an inch above the bottom, allowed waste to fall through drainage holes drilled into the steel. The chamber was equipped with a food box and a water-bottle holder and was covered with a pyramid-shaped top designed to prevent the monkeys from hanging from the upper part of the chamber. Harlow placed infant monkeys in the chamber alone for periods of up to six weeks. Within a few days, the monkeys ceased moving and remained huddled in a corner. Upon removal from the chamber, the monkeys exhibited psychotic behavior, and most did not recover. Harlow's earlier experiments on the effects of loneliness involved isolating monkeys in cages surrounded by steel walls with a small one-way mirror. This setup allowed the experimenters to observe the monkeys without the monkeys being able to see out. The only interaction the monkeys had with the outside world occurred when experimenters changed their bedding or provided food and water. Infant monkeys were placed in these isolation boxes shortly after birth. Four monkeys were isolated for 30 days, four for six months, and four for a year. After 30 days, the total isolates, as they were called, were described as enormously disturbed. After a year of isolation, the monkeys barely moved, did not explore or play, and were incapable of engaging in sexual behavior. When introduced to other monkeys for daily play sessions, they were severely bullied. Two of the monkeys refused to eat and starved themselves to death. To study how these isolates would parent, Harlow devised a device he called the rape rack, in which female isolates were restrained in a position that mimicked the natural posture of a female monkey during mating. Artificial insemination was not available at the time. Harlow found that, just as the isolates were incapable of normal sexual behavior, they were also unable to parent their offspring. The mothers either abused or neglected their infants. Harlow wrote, Not even in our most devious dreams could we have designed a surrogate as evil as these real monkey mothers were. Lacking any social experience themselves, the mothers were incapable of appropriate social interaction. One mother held her infant's face to the floor and chewed off its feet and fingers. Another crushed her infant's head. Most simply ignored their offspring. These experiments demonstrated the profound effects of total and partial isolation on developing monkeys. However, Harlow believed he had not yet captured the essence of depression, which he described as being characterized by feelings of loneliness, helplessness, and a sense of being trapped, or sunk in a well of despair. The technical name for the new depression chamber was the vertical chamber apparatus, though Harlow referred to it as the pit of despair, well of despair, dungeon of despair, and well of loneliness. Most of the monkeys placed in the chamber were at least three months old and had already formed social bonds with others. The goal of the experiment was to sever these bonds to induce symptoms of depression. According to Harlow, Most subjects typically assume a hunched position in a corner of the bottom of the apparatus. One might presume at this point that they find their situation to be hopeless. Steven Suomi, one of Harlow's doctoral students, placed monkeys in the chamber for his Ph.D. research. He reported that no monkey exhibited any defense against the chamber's effects. Even the happiest monkeys emerged profoundly damaged. Suomi concluded that even a happy, normal childhood offered no protection against depression. The experiments yielded what science writer Deborah Blum described as common sense results: that monkeys, being highly social animals, suffer severe psychological damage when placed in isolation, and that some recover while others do not. William Mason, another of Harlow's students, later reflected on the work, stating that Harlow kept this going to the point where it was clear to many people that the work was really violating ordinary sensibilities, that anybody with respect for life or people would find this offensive. Mason suggested that Harlow's later work seemed almost intentionally provocative, as if he wanted to leave behind a controversial legacy. If that was his aim, he did a perfect job, Mason remarked.
